transcript:
Fireflies.ai Transcript

Meeting: VectorForge x Redwood Inference — Discovery (code assistant + structured outputs)
Date: May 17, 2025
Time: 10:02 AM PT
Duration: 46 min
Recorded by: Fireflies.ai

Attendees
Redwood Inference: Hannah Schmitt (AE), Simran Kaur (Solutions Architect)
VectorForge: Evan Brooks (Head of Product), Mina Patel (Staff ML Engineer), Jonas Lindström (Platform Engineer)

Summary (auto-generated)
VectorForge described a production code-assistant workload (IDE plugin + web app) where low latency, predictable formatting, and strong reliability are critical. They prefer open-weight models for controllability and cost, but they need structured output (JSON) and tool/function calling patterns that don’t break under streaming. Redwood reviewed hosted vs dedicated options, how structured output is handled, and what benchmark data is needed to validate performance. The group aligned on a follow-up technical deep dive and a small benchmark plan using VectorForge prompts.

Topics (auto-generated)
- Current stack and model mix for code assistant
- Structured output / JSON schema reliability
- Streaming stability and partial JSON issues
- Preference for open models vs proprietary APIs
- Latency targets (p50/p95), throughput, and burst behavior
- Evaluation approach and benchmark plan
- Potential for a performance-focused customer story

Questions (auto-generated)
- How does Redwood enforce or improve JSON / schema adherence in streaming mode?
- Can we pin a model version and roll back quickly if quality regresses?
- What’s the expected behavior under burst traffic (rate limits, queuing, fallbacks)?
- Which open models does Redwood support that are strong for code tasks?

Action items (auto-generated)
- Redwood to send structured output requirement checklist and propose a benchmark plan.
- VectorForge to provide representative prompts, schemas, and baseline metrics.
- Schedule technical deep dive to discuss architecture and SLOs.


Transcript

[00:00] Hannah Schmitt: Cool, thanks everyone for making time. I’m Hannah, I run a bunch of our dev tools and infra accounts. Simran’s here as well, she’ll probably jump in on the technical bits.

[00:10] Simran Kaur: Hey everyone.

[00:12] Evan Brooks: Hey, I’m Evan. I run product for VectorForge.

[00:15] Mina Patel: Mina, ML engineering.

[00:17] Jonas Lindström: Jonas, platform.

[00:20] Hannah Schmitt: Awesome. So the goal today is like, understand your workload, what you’re using now, what’s not working, and then see if it makes sense to do a pilot with Redwood. If it does, we can set up a deep dive and define acceptance criteria. Sound good?

[00:33] Evan Brooks: Yep.

[00:34] Hannah Schmitt: Great. Evan, maybe start high level—what is VectorForge building and where inference shows up.

[00:42] Evan Brooks: Sure. We do a code assistant. It’s basically an IDE extension and a web experience. Think inline completions, chat about codebase, and some agent-ish workflows where it runs tools—like search, build a patch, run tests, that kind of thing.

[00:59] Hannah Schmitt: Got it.

[01:00] Evan Brooks: The big thing for us is we can’t have it hang. Like a dev is typing and it has to feel snappy. And then for the agent workflows, it has to produce structured outputs because it’s calling internal tools. When it returns, it needs to be valid JSON. Not “mostly JSON.”

[01:18] Mina Patel: Yeah, and we do streaming. So we have the additional fun problem that partial JSON is… it’s like it breaks parsers unless you buffer, and then buffering kills perceived latency. So we’ve tried a few patterns.

[01:33] Simran Kaur: Makes sense. When you say structured, are you using like function calling style, or strict JSON schema, or both?

[01:40] Mina Patel: Both-ish. For the agent, we’re basically doing a schema. It’s like {"tool": "…", "arguments": {…}}. And then sometimes it returns an array of tool calls.

[01:52] Jonas Lindström: And then for some tasks we want just a JSON blob with fields, like change summary, file paths, diff hunks, etc.

[02:01] Hannah Schmitt: Understood. Can I ask what you’re using today? Like which providers / stack.

[02:07] Mina Patel: It’s a mix. We have OpenAI for some high-accuracy stuff. We’ve tried Anthropic too. For cost reasons and control we run open models in our own Kubernetes cluster for the bulk—varies by customer tier.

[02:23] Evan Brooks: And we’re trying to consolidate because the operational burden is annoying. Especially during bursts.

[02:29] Jonas Lindström: It’s like, we can keep it alive but we spend too much time tuning GPU nodes and queueing. Also, we have this thing where we want to pin a model version because any regression is a support nightmare. With some providers it’s… not stable.

[02:45] Hannah Schmitt: Yep. Version pinning is a core use case for us. We let you pin by model version, and then you can do a canary or rollback. That’s the Console rollouts piece.

[02:55] Evan Brooks: Okay.

[02:56] Hannah Schmitt: On the open models point—our whole thing is we support a curated catalog of open models and we’ll host them, or do dedicated capacity, or private. For dev tools we see a lot of customers want open weights.

[03:10] Mina Patel: The question is like, will the structured output actually work. We’ve been burned.

[03:16] Simran Kaur: Totally fair. Let’s dig in. Two parts: (1) model behavior—some models are just better at schema adherence; (2) serving/runtime behavior—things like stopping criteria, streaming chunking, and optionally constrained decoding, depending on approach.

[03:33] Mina Patel: When you say constrained decoding, do you mean like actual JSON grammar constraints?

[03:37] Simran Kaur: There are levels. Some customers do strict grammar-based decoding. Some do “soft constraints” with sampling controls and post-validation + retries. We support structured output modes that can do schema validation and retry policies, and we can advise on model choice.

[03:53] Jonas Lindström: Is that in the API? Like we can pass a schema?

[03:56] Simran Kaur: Yes. In our chat/generation endpoint you can pass a structured output spec. The exact parameter names depend on SDK vs REST, but you can supply JSON schema and request strict mode. If it fails validation, you can configure a retry count. For streaming, we typically recommend one of two patterns: either stream tokens but buffer until a valid JSON object boundary, or stream and provide a “final” event that is guaranteed valid JSON.

[04:22] Mina Patel: That “final event” model is what we do now with one provider. But sometimes the model emits garbage before it gets to final.

[04:29] Simran Kaur: Right, and that’s why you want the tooling layer to treat the earlier stream as non-authoritative and only commit when you get a validated final payload. If you also need the UX to feel responsive, you can stream a “thought-lite” text channel separately from the JSON channel. Some teams do dual channel.

[04:49] Evan Brooks: We’ve avoided “thoughts” for obvious reasons. But streaming a user-friendly status is okay.

[04:56] Hannah Schmitt: On the product side, we don’t require you to show chain-of-thought. Just to be clear.

[05:01] Evan Brooks: Good.

[05:03] Hannah Schmitt: Let’s talk SLOs. What are you trying to hit latency-wise? Like p50, p95.

[05:10] Mina Patel: For inline completions, it’s super tight. We’d like p50 under 250ms to first token, p95 under maybe 700ms. But that’s region dependent.

[05:22] Jonas Lindström: For agent tasks, we can tolerate more. But we have a “no hanging” thing. Like if it times out or returns 429 we get churn.

[05:33] Hannah Schmitt: Makes sense. On our side we usually separate first-token latency vs full completion. Also, what token lengths are typical?

[05:41] Mina Patel: Inline is small—like 30 to 120 tokens. Agent tasks can be huge. Sometimes it’s like 800 to 2k tokens because it’s writing patch diffs.

[05:53] Simran Kaur: And context length? Are you sending repo context, retrieval, etc.?

[05:58] Mina Patel: We chunk and retrieve. But yes, we can hit 16k sometimes. For some customers it’s 32k.

[06:06] Simran Kaur: Okay. That will matter for model choice and batching/caching. Do you have a lot of shared prefixes? Like same system prompt across many requests.

[06:16] Mina Patel: Yes. System prompt is identical across users per product version. Then there’s per-user context and retrieved docs.

[06:24] Simran Kaur: Great—prefix caching can help there.

[06:27] Jonas Lindström: We do some caching now but it’s homegrown.

[06:31] Hannah Schmitt: Understood. Another thing: do you need dedicated capacity for predictability or are you okay with multi-tenant hosted?

[06:38] Evan Brooks: We’re open. We have some enterprise customers who would prefer dedicated or at least data isolation. But we also want a quick win. Maybe start hosted, then dedicate for the high tiers.

[06:53] Hannah Schmitt: That’s pretty common. We can do Hosted API to get you moving, and then Dedicated pools for predictable throughput.

[07:01] Jonas Lindström: Are there fallbacks? Like if the pool is saturated.

[07:05] Simran Kaur: Yes. Smart routing and fallback policies. You can define primary model and fallback model variants or regions. For example: primary open model A in us-west, fallback same model in us-east, or fallback to a slightly smaller model with a “degraded mode” tag.

[07:23] Mina Patel: That’s interesting. We do a similar thing but we built it ourselves and it’s… brittle.

[07:30] Hannah Schmitt: Yeah. And for messaging—we’re running a case study + design partner program where we want performance-focused stories. If the pilot goes well and you’re comfortable, we’d love to feature VectorForge. But that’s totally optional and later.

[07:44] Evan Brooks: We might be interested, but it depends on the results and what we can share. We’re okay talking about performance outcomes. We don’t want to expose customer names or proprietary prompts.

[07:56] Hannah Schmitt: That’s totally fine. We can keep it high-level and focus on outcomes and architecture patterns. We’ll run it through your approval.

[08:06] Mina Patel: We’re more likely to do it if it’s like “we cut p95 by X” or “we reduced cost per completion.” Not fluff.

[08:13] Hannah Schmitt: That is exactly the angle.

[08:15] Simran Kaur: On that note, what’s your baseline today? Do you have numbers? Even rough.

[08:21] Mina Patel: Roughly… for self-hosted, p95 can be like 1.2s first token during peak. Off-peak it’s fine, like 400ms. Cost wise it’s hard because we amortize GPUs and it’s not clean.

[08:37] Jonas Lindström: And for OpenAI, latency is okay but cost is… yeah. Also compliance wise some customers ask questions.

[08:46] Hannah Schmitt: Understood. We can help you get to a clean cost-per-request metric using our Console and your usage windows.

[08:55] Simran Kaur: For structured output, can you tell me the failure modes you’ve seen? Like invalid JSON, missing fields, wrong types, etc.?

[09:04] Mina Patel: All of the above. The most annoying is trailing commas, or it returns markdown fences like ```json. Or it returns “Sure, here’s the JSON:” plus text. And then type mismatch, like “lineNumbers” is a string.

[09:21] Simran Kaur: Yep. We typically enforce “no markdown” via system prompt and stop sequences, and then strict schema validation. If it fails, we retry with a correction prompt like “Return ONLY valid JSON matching schema; do not include prose.”

[09:37] Mina Patel: Retries add latency though.

[09:39] Simran Kaur: They do. The goal is to pick a model + decoding settings where retries are rare. Another trick is to keep temperature low for JSON generation and separate creative parts from structured parts.

[09:54] Evan Brooks: We do that sometimes. But it’s hard to manage.

[09:58] Hannah Schmitt: That’s a big part of why customers come to us—make it consistent across routes.

[10:04] Jonas Lindström: How do you handle rate limits? Because we get 429s from a provider and it’s like… it cascades.

[10:11] Hannah Schmitt: For Hosted API we have quotas and rate limits you can configure, and we can work with you on a predictable baseline. For Dedicated you get reserved throughput; you still need client-side backoff, but 429s should be far less frequent because capacity is allocated.

[10:28] Simran Kaur: Also, we can set queueing policies—like maximum queue delay. If queue delay exceeds, you can trigger fallback rather than waiting.

[10:38] Mina Patel: That’s nice. Because “hanging” is the worst UX.

[10:41] Hannah Schmitt: Exactly.

[10:44] Evan Brooks: Model support—do you have, like, code-specific open models? Or do we bring our own?

[10:50] Simran Kaur: We have several code-capable open models in the catalog, and we can onboard additional ones if needed, depending on licensing and demand. Typically we’d start with 2–3 candidates and benchmark on your prompts.

[11:05] Mina Patel: We care about “open weights” specifically. Also, we want the option to run in our own VPC later.

[11:12] Hannah Schmitt: Yep. We support private deployment as well. But for a first step, Hosted or Dedicated is fastest.

[11:20] Jonas Lindström: If we do Hosted first, can we later move to Dedicated without changing the API?

[11:25] Hannah Schmitt: Same API, yes. You’d change an endpoint or a project setting; your integration stays the same.

[11:33] Mina Patel: That matters.

[11:35] Simran Kaur: For the benchmark, what would you consider success? Like acceptance thresholds.

[11:42] Mina Patel: For inline, if we can consistently hit p95 under 700ms first token in us-west, I’d be happy. For agent tasks, more like stable streaming and no schema breakage above, say, 99.5%.

[11:58] Evan Brooks: And cost. If it’s not meaningfully cheaper than what we’re doing, it’s hard to justify switching.

[12:06] Hannah Schmitt: Understood. In pilots we usually set 2–3 key metrics: latency, error rate, and cost per request or per token. And then we define the measurement window.

[12:19] Jonas Lindström: We also need to talk about what happens when there’s an incident. Like who’s on call.

[12:23] Hannah Schmitt: For Dedicated and enterprise tiers, we have SLAs and support response times. For Hosted, there’s still support but the SLA differs. We can cover that in the deep dive.

[12:36] Mina Patel: Do you have audit logs? Not sure if that’s relevant for us, but some customers ask.

[12:41] Hannah Schmitt: We do. And for private/VPC there’s more controls. But since you’re not regulated like healthcare, it might be lighter.

[12:50] Evan Brooks: Some of our customers are banks, so it comes up.

[12:55] Hannah Schmitt: Got it.

[13:00] Simran Kaur: Quick question on request shape: are you doing single request per user action, or do you do parallel tool calls and multiple completions?

[13:08] Mina Patel: For agent, multiple. It’ll call retrieval, then call the model, then call tools. Sometimes we do n=2 completions and pick best.

[13:18] Simran Kaur: That impacts throughput and batching. Good to know.

[13:23] Jonas Lindström: Also, we do “speculative” calls sometimes—like send a fast model and a slow model.

[13:29] Simran Kaur: We can support routing policies like that. Again, depends on the deployment.

[13:36] Hannah Schmitt: Can I ask timeline? Like when would you want to start, if we can hit the goals?

[13:42] Evan Brooks: Ideally in the next month. We have a release in six weeks.

[13:47] Mina Patel: But we can start testing sooner. We just need time to integrate.

[13:52] Hannah Schmitt: That’s reasonable. Typically we can get you keys same day, then it’s a week or two to run a meaningful benchmark.

[14:01] Jonas Lindström: If we need Dedicated, does that take longer?

[14:04] Hannah Schmitt: A bit. Hosted is instant; Dedicated depends on region and capacity but we can usually do a pilot quickly if we scope it.

[14:14] Mina Patel: Can we do hosted for the benchmark but with some guarantee? Because we don’t want noisy neighbors to skew results.

[14:21] Simran Kaur: For an initial benchmark, hosted can still be informative, but yes, for strict p95 you might want Dedicated. Another approach is we can run a controlled benchmark window and isolate it. We can talk internally.

[14:38] Hannah Schmitt: Yeah, we can figure out the right plan.

[14:41] Evan Brooks: On the case study thing, just to circle back—if we do it, it has to be performance-focused and we’d want to review it. Also maybe we’d prefer “customer story” not “design partner” language.

[14:54] Hannah Schmitt: Totally. And nothing goes public without your written approval.

[14:59] Mina Patel: Also, we’d want to avoid saying exactly which model, if that’s a competitive thing. Or at least we’d want the option.

[15:06] Hannah Schmitt: Understood. We can anonymize certain details, or keep it at “open-weight code model.”

[15:13] Simran Kaur: For the technical deep dive, can you share 3–5 representative prompts? Ideally a mix: inline completion, chat about code, and one agent structured output.

[15:24] Mina Patel: Yes. We’ll sanitize them.

[15:27] Jonas Lindström: And we can share output schema examples.

[15:31] Hannah Schmitt: Great.

[15:33] (crosstalk)

[15:34] Evan Brooks: One concern we have: vendor lock-in. Like if we build to your structured output mode and then later we want to switch.

[15:43] Simran Kaur: Good question. We try to align with common patterns—JSON schema, tool call style. We’re not doing something completely proprietary. And you can keep your prompts and schemas; the transport is standard.

[15:58] Hannah Schmitt: And since we support multiple models/deployments, you’re not locked to one provider’s proprietary model.

[16:05] Mina Patel: That’s appealing.

[16:07] Jonas Lindström: Another thing: we need to know how you handle data retention. Some providers keep prompts.

[16:13] Hannah Schmitt: For enterprise tiers we have configurable retention and no training on your data. We can share specifics in follow-up and the security docs.

[16:22] Evan Brooks: Okay.

[16:24] Simran Kaur: Let me ask about concurrency. How many requests per second at peak, roughly?

[16:30] Jonas Lindström: It varies. Inline completions can spike to 200–300 rps. Agent tasks are lower, like 10–20 rps but heavier.

[16:41] Simran Kaur: That mix is common. We can tune batching differently per route.

[16:47] Mina Patel: We also have geographic distribution—US mostly, some EU.

[16:52] Hannah Schmitt: We have regions in NA and EU. If EU data residency is needed, we can support that depending on tier.

[17:00] Evan Brooks: For now, EU is not strict, but we might need it later.

[17:06] Hannah Schmitt: Okay.

[17:08] Simran Kaur: On structured outputs: do you need deterministic fields? Like ordering, whitespace.

[17:13] Mina Patel: Not ordering, but types yes. And no extra fields ideally.

[17:18] Simran Kaur: We can validate for allowed properties and types.

[17:22] Mina Patel: Cool.

[17:23] Hannah Schmitt: Switching gears a little—procurement/security. If we do a pilot, do you need to start with an NDA or security review?

[17:31] Evan Brooks: NDA yes. Security review maybe if it goes to enterprise tier. For pilot, we can be lighter, but we’ll still ask questions.

[17:40] Jonas Lindström: We’ll need your SOC2 report eventually.

[17:43] Hannah Schmitt: Yep, we can provide under NDA.

[17:47] (brief audio drop)

[17:50] Mina Patel: Sorry, can you repeat the last part? Audio cut.

[17:53] Hannah Schmitt: Yeah—SOC2 report we can share under NDA.

[17:58] Mina Patel: Got it.

[18:01] Simran Kaur: One more question: Are you doing any fine-tuning today?

[18:05] Mina Patel: Not fine-tuning. Prompting + retrieval. We might consider LoRA later.

[18:10] Simran Kaur: Okay. For inference only, that simplifies.

[18:14] Hannah Schmitt: Alright. I think we’ve got enough for next steps. Let’s propose a technical deep dive. Simran will lead. We’ll also send a checklist for structured output requirements so you can confirm what matters—schema strictness, retries, streaming behavior.

[18:31] Evan Brooks: Sounds good.

[18:33] Hannah Schmitt: Mina, can you share sample prompts and schemas? Even if sanitized.

[18:37] Mina Patel: Yep, we’ll do that.

[18:40] Hannah Schmitt: Jonas, can you confirm infra constraints like whether you need VPC and which region you prefer.

[18:46] Jonas Lindström: Yeah.

[18:48] Simran Kaur: And if you have any baseline metrics—p50/p95 first token, error rate, cost per request—even rough, it will help us design the benchmark.

[18:58] Mina Patel: We can pull a week of data and give ballparks.

[19:02] Hannah Schmitt: Great. Anything else you want to make sure we cover next time?

[19:07] Evan Brooks: Just want to see if you can hit the latency, and that the JSON thing doesn’t blow up.

[19:12] Mina Patel: Yeah, and open models only. That’s a hard preference for us.

[19:17] Hannah Schmitt: Understood. We’ll keep it open models in the plan.

[19:22] Simran Kaur: Cool.

[19:23] Hannah Schmitt: Thanks all. I’ll send a recap and scheduling options.

[19:28] Evan Brooks: Thanks.

[19:29] Mina Patel: Thanks.

[19:30] Jonas Lindström: Thanks.

[19:31] Meeting ended
